Why US/EU indie teams reach for ChatGPT first

The workflow is tempting: copy title, subtitle, description, and keywords from App Store Connect, paste into ChatGPT with “translate to Simplified Chinese for App Store,” paste the reply back. No invoice, no waiting. For a solo developer shipping internationally, that feels like localization checked off.

The problem is not that models translate badly in isolation — it is that store copy is a constrained product surface, not a blog post. ChatGPT optimizes for fluent paragraphs. App Store Connect optimizes for hard character caps, hidden keyword fields, Search indexing rules, and Chinese buyers who recognize machine brochure tone in one skim. Those goals conflict. A free model dump saves money on the first paste and costs you on the second — when you rewrite everything anyway.

What ChatGPT and Google Translate get wrong on zh-Hans listings

Keyword stuffing the model thinks is “ASO”

LLMs love repeating search nouns because training data includes SEO blog posts. Ask for “App Store keywords in Chinese” and you often get the same terms pasted into title, subtitle, description, and a comma-separated block — 效率, 专注, 番茄钟, 待办, 习惯 in every field. Apple’s zh-Hans storefront has a hidden 100-character keyword field plus visible title and subtitle; repeating nouns across all of them reads as spam to human buyers and wastes limited characters. Models rarely split terms the way a human operator would — synonyms in keywords, outcome in subtitle, brand plus category in title.

Character limits Connect enforces — and ChatGPT ignores

App Store Connect rejects or truncates over-limit fields. Title and subtitle are commonly capped around 30 characters each for zh-Hans; keywords around 100 characters; promotional text at 170; description up to 4,000. ChatGPT answers with no live counter tied to your locale row. You discover the overflow only when Connect flags the save — or worse, when a truncated title cuts mid-word in Search. Google Translate has the same blind spot: it translates length, not limits. Human rewrite enforces counts before you paste.

翻译腔 — fluent Chinese that still reads like a translation

Machine output often lands in formal 翻译腔: stacked adjectives (“专业 · 高效 · 智能”), false cognates (“极致体验”, “强大功能”), and English sentence order preserved in long clauses Chinese readers skip. It is grammatically Simplified Chinese and commercially dead — the tone of a manual, not an indie app a person would recommend. Chinese users on the App Store recognize template copy instantly; it signals that nobody on your team speaks to that market. A human rewrite keeps your English product personality — direct, quirky, or minimal — in idiomatic zh-Hans instead of generic brochure dialect.

Trademark and competitor-name collisions

Models happily translate “better than Notion” or “Todoist alternative” into Chinese strings that name registered marks you do not own. They also suggest Chinese renderings of global brand names that collide with local apps already ranking on those terms. Apple review and competitor complaints are not theoretical — pasted LLM output has shipped competitor trademarks into subtitle and keyword fields because the model treated them as generic nouns. Human rewrite flags cut-list items: what to remove, what to genericize, what to keep as an English loanword Chinese users actually search.

Voice drift — your English tone disappears

Your en-US listing might be short, wry, or feature-specific. ChatGPT defaults to marketing template voice in any language — the same “提升效率，掌控生活” opener on every productivity app. That erases differentiation you already earned in English. Buyers who cross-check your English and Chinese pages notice the mismatch; it reads as outsourced, not shipped. AppLocale rewrites from your English source so zh-Hans sounds like the same product, not a translation of a translation.
